An AI-assisted QC system that cut review from 14 days to 48 hours

I led CD Baby's first AI-assisted quality-control system for release review. Humans checked every release against dozens of hidden partner rules, artists waited up to two weeks, and review was our biggest source of support tickets.

Chapter 1

The problem and the conflict

The queue held about 11,700 reviews with about 1,600 new ones a day. Artists wanted hours. Operations wanted strict checks. Some leaders wanted to cut review as a cost center, but dropping below partner scorecard thresholds put platform access at risk, so I argued for fixing the process instead.

Chapter 2

What we built

Hive.ai scanned each release's metadata and artwork against the same partner rules humans used and returned a pass or fail confidence score in 45 to 60 seconds. It did not replace full-listening judgment. Low-risk releases skipped review, high-risk ones went to people, and accounts with three or more clean releases auto-passed. Artists also saw warnings at upload so they could fix issues themselves.

Chapter 3

How we earned trust

V1 was internal only, with inspectors using it and support beta-testing it. V2 showed artists only validated, high-accuracy errors. Before anything auto-approved, I agreed the trust metrics with Data Science: flag rate, false positives, rework and escalations. I set the threshold cautiously, because a bad release slipping through hurts partner report cards far more than an extra review.

Case study 2 · How I use AI day to day

Crew weren't underpaid. They just couldn't see the rule.

Overtime gap checker

Try it: a 10-hour day rate, paid two ways

How payroll is set up
What the crew quoted$5,720
What the timecard pays$5,600
$120 shortThat is $30 less per day than the quote.

Quote base $110.00 an hour, payroll base $100.00 an hour.

Illustrative: a California-style rule (overtime after 8 hours, double time after 12), without meal penalties, 6th and 7th day rules or unions.

Freelance film and photo crew kept saying a payroll platform "underpays overtime". I used AI for the research, the math, the spec and the code to find out why, and designed a fix that shows the rule when it matters. I've left the platform's name out.

Chapter 1

Finding a problem worth solving

I searched public crew and producer threads for the platform. About 85 to 90 percent of results were job posts, which left eight user threads and six I read in full. Four themes came out: overtime that doesn't match the deal, support that's hard to reach, small productions unsure who would take them, and insurance declines for stunts. Overtime was the only one that appeared for both crew and producers over two years, named the platform directly, had a cause I could explain and could be fixed with something small. AI couldn't reach the site, so I ran the searches and pasted the threads back.

Chapter 2

Learning the domain in a day

I was new to film payroll, so I had AI build me a visual crash course: one worked example, who is involved, pay hours drawn as blocks, a live explorer, vocabulary and a quiz. The calculator shows the core idea. Crew divide a $1,100 day rate by 10 hours. Payroll divides it by 11 "pay hours", because California counts hours 9 and 10 as overtime. Every overtime hour is paid on the lower base, so four 12-hour days come up $120 short, the same figure a crew member reported.

Chapter 3

The reframe: it wasn't a bug

Checking the platform's own help pages changed my direction. A setting that pays what crew quote already exists. Producers pick the setting per worker at deal setup, crew never see which one was chosen, and admins see a number without the reason. The problem was visibility, not math. So I stopped designing a calculator and started designing a way to show the existing setting in the product.

Chapter 4

The fix: turn the lights on at three moments

Pay isn't calculated any differently. The rule is simply shown where the mismatch begins, reusing patterns the product already has.

1. Warn the producerAt deal setup, a plain line says what the setting costs the crew member, then offers a one-click match.
2. Show the crewThe deal summary crew already open shows the rule, the real hourly base and what a 12-hour day pays against their quote.
3. Catch it before paydayAn "Issue" on the timecard, built on the existing alert pattern, with a hidden-rate version for roles without pay access.

How I used AI, and where I made the calls

AI did the research, math, synthesis, spec and code. I chose the direction, gathered what it couldn't reach, and pushed back when its output drifted from reality.

  1. 1. Discovery

    What happened
    AI was blocked from the site on every route.
    My call
    I ran the searches myself and pasted the results and threads back.

  2. 2. Synthesis

    What happened
    It ranked four themes, reframed "underpays" as work hours against pay hours and reproduced the $120 exactly.
    My call
    I chose overtime and checked a recent thread to prove it is still happening.

  3. 3. Docs check

    What happened
    It found that a matching setting already exists, so the problem became visibility, not math.
    My call
    I shifted the solution from "a calculator" to "show the existing setting in the product".

  4. 4. Prototype

    What happened
    Claude wrote a spec with test cases and V0 built four screens.
    My call
    I reviewed the output with Claude and found 15 issues, including inputs losing focus, state not shared across screens and a wrong timecard grid.

  5. 5. Brand check

    What happened
    I had given V0 an estimated palette. A screenshot of the real app showed a different violet.
    My call
    I corrected it from the real screenshot, not the estimate.

  6. 6. Cost control

    What happened
    I set a $6 credit cap. Claude stopped V0's self-checking run and made the remaining fixes directly in the project files.
    My call
    Total spend was about $3.17.

  7. 7. Copy review

    What happened
    The first warning opened with a fact about crew habits and listed three numbers with no conclusion.
    My call
    I couldn't follow it, and I'm close to the real user, so I rewrote it to lead with the impact, explain why in one line, then offer the fix.

What I'd do next

This was a take-home exercise, so these are proposals and not results.

  • Size the problem with the platform's own data first: support tickets that mention overtime, manual wage adjustments on overtime days, and the share of deals on a setting that doesn't match typical quotes.
  • Run five interviews each with crew and producers using the prototype.
  • Measure overtime tickets, manual adjustments and matching-setting share, and track whether crew open the "how is this calculated" panel before their first timecard.
  • Risks: premium settings cost producers more, so the warning must inform the choice, not push it, and wording needs legal review. Edge cases such as 6th and 7th days, meal penalties and blended rates weren't modeled.
  • Rollout: admin warnings first, because they carry the least risk, then crew-facing transparency.

adoption, about 2× the product it replaced

Boost: a publishing replacement from zero

I retired a publishing product that couldn't scale and launched its replacement: a $39.99 service bundling MLC, SoundExchange and sync royalties.

The full story

I oversaw Pro publishing's global expansion, then advised against scaling it for two reasons: the partner could not handle the volume, and the outdated program needed a major overhaul that would have cost more resources to modernize than to rebuild. When it wound down, existing Pro clients were fully grandfathered and received Boost at no extra cost. For new users, Boost offered a more flexible a la carte selection with more advanced royalty choices and payouts. Artists could opt in one songwriter or artist on a track and not another, and set a different royalty percentage for each opted-in person, track by track. The old product only allowed track-by-track selection, with no percentage per songwriter or artist.

The 42% adoption figure is measured on the cart upsell: of the users shown it, the share who chose to add Boost to their regular release submission.

Operations
About 40%
cut from the inspection backlog in each of two flushes

Clearing backlogs without risking partner access

I cleared a large inspection backlog by auto-approving accounts with a clean track record, so partner quality scores stayed safe.

The full story

I ran two flushes at different times, each using the same clean-account auto-pass logic as the AI quality-control system: accounts with a clean history skipped manual review, and risky releases still went to a person. The first took the queue from about 8,200 to about 4,600. The queue later climbed back, and the second flush started from close to 10,000 and cut it by about 40% again. An earlier April flush also cut about 40% and generated only about 14 Apple tickets, which showed the approach was safe before I repeated it. Separately, I cleared an aged support queue of about 17.8K tickets: a purge of resolved, duplicate and stale tickets, each sent a “reply if you still need help” message, removed about 90% of it, and the platform and automation fixes stopped it from refilling.

Security and support

Account recovery that lets real owners back in

Fewer lockout tickets, without opening the door to attackers

Problem
Many artists log in once a year or less. By then their email, phone or address has often changed, so they contacted support to get back in. Login tickets were one of the biggest ticket drivers after release inspection.
What I did
I owned the change end to end and engineering built it. Recovery is risk scored: low-risk requests are approved automatically and higher-risk ones go to a person. It includes texted codes, a forced refresh of stale details, rate limits against SMS abuse and breached-password checks. I prototyped the flow in V0 and wrote the requirements.
Rollout
Web, for every user going through the login flow.
27%fewer tickets from these requests over 90 days

Prototypes

I prototype in V0 so ideas get tested before build

Working screens help engineers, designers and stakeholders react to something real. V0 even generated full requirements for every page from my admin portal prototype.

Inside the admin tools prototype

A prototype for support and operations teams: find any account, change many at once, act safely on one, and manage a global catalog. It uses mock data, identifiers are redacted, and V0 generated a full requirements document for every page from the finished screens.

Adding a contributor, one question at a time

A prototype for the customer side of a music platform: how someone adds a songwriter, producer or performer to their account. One decision per screen, a branch on who the person already is, and the rights details tucked into optional sections so a first-timer is never blocked. The screens use test data.

Who gets paid: credits and splits

Prototype screens for the part of a release where money gets divided: songwriter shares that have to total 100%, payment splits on an artist profile, and a confirm or decline step for splits on releases someone else owns. All data is mock and the names are placeholders.

Game design case study, in progress

Seasons & Scandal: a Regency dynasty sim I am designing end to end

You guide one family through generations of London Seasons. Plan each spring, marry off the children, survive the gossip pages, and watch traits surface, hide and return down the bloodline. I wrote the design doc, built a playable prototype in V0, and art-directed the look with AI image tools. It is a personal project, portfolio first, with Steam as the long-term goal.

The problem

Dynasty games often bury their genetics in hidden numbers. I wanted inheritance that players can see, plan around and still be surprised by.

My role

Systems design, UX and UI, writing, and art direction. I own the design doc, the prototype and the visual style guide.

Approach

Design doc and parts list first. A V0 prototype to test the core loop. Then concept sheets made with AI tools, cleaned up by hand in Krita and Photoshop.

The playable prototype

Portrait system and art direction

Design choices so far

  • Face shapes and features come whole from one parent. Skin tone, hair color and hair texture come from either parent or land in between.
  • Eye color follows dominant and recessive rules, and rare conditions can run in families.
  • Five body builds, with hidden builds that unlock only through inherited conditions.
  • Charm and wit are inherited, but accomplishment is learned, so education matters.
  • Families carry succession laws, entailed estates and heirlooms.

Status: playable prototype with one family. Next up: the layered portrait pipeline and the founding character creator.
